mainTopic: Walls and breaches on שבת: two courtyards whose dividing wall fell, a courtyard breached into the רשות הרבים, and places that lost their walls during שבת.
overview: This amud opens with the end of the מחלוקת between רב and שמואל about a wall between two courtyards that fell on שבת. שמואל says each side may carry up to the base of the fallen wall. The גמרא explains that רב's stricter view was learned from a story. רב turned his face away when שמואל had a cloak hung on the wall. The גמרא then answers why שמואל needed the cloak (only for privacy), and why רב only turned away and did not speak up (it was שמואל's town, but he did not want people to think he had changed his mind). Next comes a new משנה about a courtyard breached into the רשות הרבים. רבי אליעזר treats it as public domain, and the חכמים call it a כרמלית. The גמרא gives two explanations of רבי אליעזר: a lost public path, or the rule that the edges of a public domain count as public domain. It then defends the second explanation against challenges from the wording 'מתוכה'. A last משנה has רבי יהודה and רבי יוסי arguing about places that lost their walls during שבת. The גמרא asks how wide the breach must be, and רב's answer begins at the end of the amud and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: שמואל's ruling: each side may carry up to the base of the fallen wall
steps.stepSummary: שמואל rules that after a wall between two courtyards falls on שבת, each courtyard's residents may still carry up to where the wall used to stand.
steps.simpleTranslation: This one may carry up to the base of the wall, and that one may carry up to the base of the wall.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the end of the dispute. It gives שמואל's side: even though the wall fell, each courtyard may carry right up to where the wall stood.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל's reasoning is that the courtyards were permitted for carrying when שבת began, so they stay permitted for the whole שבת (שבת הואיל והותרה הותרה). רב, in the line on the previous amud, limits carrying to four אמות, because the courtyards are now open to each other without an ערוב.

keyTerms.meaning: the base of the partition, where the wall used to stand

steps.whyThisMatters: Everything that follows next is measured against this ruling. The קשיא in Step 5 quotes it word for word, and Step 6 answers it.

phrases.english: This one may carry up to the base of the partition,
phrases.notes: Each courtyard keeps its old boundary, even though the wall is gone.

phrases.english: and that one may carry up to the base of the partition.
phrases.notes: The second courtyard has the same right.

steps.triggerLanguage: זֶה מְטַלְטֵל עַד עִיקַּר מְחִיצָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the רב–שמואל dispute that began on the previous amud.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After the wall falls, each courtyard may still carry up to the line where the wall stood.

steps.title: רב's ruling was inferred, not stated outright
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that רב never said his four-אמות ruling explicitly. It was deduced from his behavior.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this ruling of רב was not stated explicitly; rather, it was stated by inference.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses to explain where רב's ruling comes from. This line sets up the story that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a difference between a ruling a חכם says in words and one his students work out from his actions. The גמרא is telling us that רב's view is a conclusion drawn from what he did, so we need to see the story to judge it.

keyTerms.meaning: by inference, deduced from something else

steps.confusionAlert: This line does not mean רב's opinion is doubtful or made up. It only tells us how we learned it: from an action, not from a statement.

phrases.english: And this ruling of Rav was not stated explicitly,
rather, it was stated by inference.
phrases.notes: His students deduced it from the story that follows.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא דְּרַב לָאו בְּפֵירוּשׁ אִתְּמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the content of the dispute to the source of רב's side of it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב's four-אמות ruling comes from an inference, not an explicit statement.

steps.title: The story: the wall falls and שמואל says to hang a cloak
steps.stepSummary: רב and שמואל were sitting in a courtyard when the wall between it and the next courtyard fell. שמואל told people to hang a cloak on what remained of the wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: For רב and שמואל were sitting in a certain courtyard, and the wall in between fell. שמואל said to them: Take a cloak and hang it on it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells the story that is the source of רב's ruling. Here שמואל gives his instruction, and this sets up רב's reaction in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Hanging the cloak makes a kind of makeshift divider between the two courtyards. To hang it, someone must carry the cloak around the courtyard. That act of carrying is what רב will react to.

keyTerms.meaning: that was in between (the two courtyards)

phrases.aramaic: דְּרַב וּשְׁמוּאֵל הֲווֹ יָתְבִי בְּהָהוּא חָצֵר,
phrases.english: For Rav and Shmuel were sitting in a certain courtyard,
and the wall in between fell,
phrases.notes: This happened on שבת.

phrases.english: Shmuel said to them:
Take a cloak and stretch it out on it.
phrases.notes: Hang it on what is left of the wall, as a divider.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּרַב וּשְׁמוּאֵל הֲווֹ יָתְבִי בְּהָהוּא חָצֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the story that step 2 said would be the source of רב's ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שמואל instructs people to carry a cloak and hang it on the remains of the fallen wall.

steps.title: רב turns his face away, and שמואל answers with a joke
steps.stepSummary: רב turns away in disapproval. From this the students learned that רב forbids carrying beyond four אמות. שמואל jokingly says to use רב's own belt to tie the cloak.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב turned his face away. שמואל said to them: If Abba is particular, take his belt and tie it with it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב silently shows he disagrees, and this is the action his students learned his ruling from. שמואל responds playfully.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Turning away showed that רב held it was forbidden to carry the cloak through the courtyard. That only makes sense if carrying is limited to four אמות, so this is the inference step 2 described. "אבא" was רב's actual name (אבא אריכא). שמואל's joke about using רב's own belt is a friendly jab: if רב is so strict, his belt can take part in the job too.

keyTerms.meaning: he turned his face away (a sign of disapproval)

steps.confusionAlert: "אבא" here does not mean "father." It is רב's own name (אבא אריכא).
steps.whatToRemember: רב's four-אמות ruling comes from his silent disapproval of carrying the cloak, not from anything he said.

phrases.english: Rav turned his face away.
phrases.notes: His students inferred his ruling from this gesture.

phrases.english: Shmuel said to them:
If Abba is particular,
phrases.notes: אבא is רב's name.

phrases.english: take his belt and tie it with it.
phrases.notes: Said with humor: use רב's belt to tie up the cloak.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַהְדְּרִינְהוּ רַב לְאַפֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows רב's reaction to שמואל's instruction, which is the basis for the inference mentioned in step 2.
steps.raayaObject: רב's ruling that one may carry only within four אמות after the wall falls.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב turning his face away when people were told to carry the cloak.

steps.title: Why did שמואל need the cloak at all?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the story: שמואל already permits carrying up to the base of the fallen wall, so the cloak seems unnecessary.
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to שמואל, why do I need this? He said: This one may carry up to the base of the partition, and that one may carry up to the base of the partition!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a question against שמואל. His own ruling seems to make hanging the cloak pointless.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the courtyards stay permitted up to the old wall line even without the wall, nothing needs to be fixed. So why put up a cloak as a divider? The גמרא quotes שמואל's ruling from step 1 word for word to show the contradiction. The answer comes next.

phrases.english: And according to Shmuel, why do I need this?
phrases.notes: "This" means hanging the cloak.

phrases.english: But he said:
This one may carry up to the base of the partition
and that one may carry up to the base of the partition!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלִשְׁמוּאֵל לְמָה לִי הָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from what the story proves about רב to a difficulty the story raises about שמואל.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's instruction to hang the cloak (step 3).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שמואל's own ruling (step 1) already allows carrying up to the old wall line without any divider, so the cloak seems unnecessary.

steps.title: שמואל hung the cloak only for privacy
steps.stepSummary: The cloak was not needed to permit carrying. שמואל hung it only to block the neighbors' view.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל did it only for privacy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 5. שמואל did not need the cloak for carrying. He hung it so the people in the other courtyard could not see into his.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumed the cloak was a halachic fix for carrying. The answer says it had a different purpose: צניעות, meaning privacy. So שמואל's rule that one may carry up to the base of the fallen wall still stands, and the cloak does not contradict it.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the cloak counts as a new wall that permits carrying. The גמרא says clearly that it was only for privacy.

phrases.english: Shmuel did it merely for privacy.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁמוּאֵל עָבֵיד לִצְנִיעוּתָא בְּעָלְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא in Step 5
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the purpose of an action
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The cloak was hung to permit carrying
steps.terutzMaskana: The cloak was hung for privacy only, so שמואל's ruling stays consistent

steps.title: Why did רב not object out loud?
steps.stepSummary: If רב held that carrying was forbidden, he should have said so to שמואל directly.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב, if he holds that it is forbidden, let him say so to him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now questions רב's side of the story. If he really disagreed, why did he only turn away instead of speaking up?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a חכם who sees others acting against his view should tell them openly. רב's silence seems strange if he truly held that carrying was אסור. This also weakens the proof from Step 4, which relied only on his body language.

phrases.english: And Rav, if he holds that it is forbidden —
let him say so to him!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַב, אִי סְבִירָא לֵיהּ דַּאֲסִיר לֵימָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from שמואל's behavior to רב's behavior
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Someone who holds a thing is forbidden should say so openly, not just turn away

steps.title: It was שמואל's town
steps.stepSummary: רב stayed quiet because they were in שמואל's place, where שמואל was the halachic authority.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was שמואל's place.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רב did not speak up because it was שמואל's town. There, שמואל's rulings were followed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A visiting חכם does not overrule the local authority in his own area. That respect for שמואל's אתרא explains why רב said nothing, even though he disagreed.

keyTerms.meaning: His place, his area of authority

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows the important principle of מרא דאתרא: in a rabbi's own town, people follow his ruling and visiting rabbis do not openly argue.

phrases.english: It was Shmuel's place.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַתְרֵיהּ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל הֲוָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא in Step 7
steps.terutzMaskana: In שמואל's town, רב deferred to him and did not argue

steps.title: Then why did רב turn his face away?
steps.stepSummary: If רב deferred to שמואל's authority, why did he show disapproval at all?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, what is the reason he turned his face away?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the last answer. If רב was showing respect to שמואל, turning his face away seems like a public protest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in Step 8 says רב deferred to שמואל. But turning away looks like the opposite of deferring. The גמרא asks how both can be true together.

phrases.english: If so, what is the reason
did he turn his face away?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, מַאי טַעְמָא אַהְדְּרִינְהוּ לְאַפֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the תירוץ in Step 8
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 8 that רב deferred to שמואל
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Turning away is a sign of protest, which does not fit with deferring to the local authority

steps.title: So people would not think רב changed his view
steps.stepSummary: רב turned away so people would not think he agreed with שמואל and had dropped his own ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: So that people would not say he holds like שמואל and retracted his ruling.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that turning away was a quiet signal. רב would not argue, but he did not want anyone to think he had given up his own opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Silence alone could be read as agreement. Turning his face away kept respect for שמואל, since he said nothing, and also protected רב's own position. So the proof in Step 4 still works: רב forbids carrying beyond four אמות.
steps.whatToRemember: The story stays consistent on both sides. שמואל hung the cloak only for privacy, and he really does permit carrying up to the fallen wall. רב truly forbids carrying beyond four אמות. He stayed silent out of respect for שמואל's town, but turned away so no one would think he had changed his mind.

phrases.english: So that they would not say
that he holds like Shmuel
(and that he retracted from his ruling).

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּלָא נֵימְרוּ כִּשְׁמוּאֵל סְבִירָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא in Step 9
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explaining the purpose of an action
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Turning away was an open protest against שמואל
steps.terutzMaskana: Turning away only showed that רב had not changed his view. It was not a challenge to שמואל's authority

steps.title: A courtyard broken open to the public domain
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה: according to רבי אליעזר, a courtyard breached into the רשות הרבים becomes public, so carrying between it and a רשות היחיד makes one חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: A courtyard that was breached into the public domain: one who carries from it into a private domain, or from a private domain into it, is liable. These are the words of רבי אליעזר.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It discusses a courtyard whose wall broke open toward the public street, and what that does to its status on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the courtyard is wide open to the רשות הרבים, רבי אליעזר treats it as part of the רשות הרבים. So moving an object between it and a private domain counts as carrying between domains on a Torah level, and the person is חייב. The words "דברי רבי אליעזר" hint that others will disagree.

keyTerms.meaning: Liable (here, for a Torah violation of carrying)

steps.confusionAlert: Here "רשות היחיד" means a different private area, like a house. It does not mean the breached courtyard itself, which is now treated as public.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
A courtyard that was breached into the public domain —
phrases.notes: Sefaria's translation explains the breach as more than ten אמות wide, so it cannot count as a doorway.

phrases.english: one who brings an object from inside it into the private domain,
or from the private domain into it —
is liable. These are the words of Rabbi Eliezer.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ חָצֵר שֶׁנִּפְרְצָה לִרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה on a related topic: a breach into the public domain instead of a breach between two courtyards
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי אליעזר, a courtyard breached into the רשות הרבים takes on public status, so carrying between it and a רשות היחיד makes one חייב

steps.title: The חכמים say the breached courtyard is like a כרמלית
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים disagree with רבי אליעזר. Carrying between the breached courtyard and the רשות הרבים is פטור, because the courtyard is only like a כרמלית.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the Rabbis say: if someone carries from inside the courtyard into the public domain, or from the public domain into it, he is exempt, because the courtyard is like a כרמלית.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה finishes by giving the view of the חכמים, who argue with רבי אליעזר from Step 11.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides agree that the breach means the courtyard is no longer a רשות היחיד. The question is what it turns into. רבי אליעזר says it becomes a full רשות הרבים. The חכמים say it becomes an in-between area, a כרמלית, so carrying from it into the רשות הרבים does not bring a Torah-level חיוב.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis, meaning the majority view that argues with רבי אליעזר
Exempt; no Torah-level liability (it may still be forbidden מדרבנן)
An in-between domain that is neither private nor fully public; carrying there is only forbidden מדרבנן

steps.confusionAlert: Here פטור does not mean 'allowed.' It only means there is no Torah-level חיוב. Carrying into or out of a כרמלית is still forbidden by the Rabbis.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis say:
from inside it (the courtyard) into the public domain
or from the public domain into it
is exempt, because it is like a karmelit.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing view to רבי אליעזר's ruling in the same משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the חכמים, a breached courtyard has the status of a כרמלית. Carrying between it and the רשות הרבים is פטור.

steps.title: Does a breach really make the courtyard public?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens by asking with surprise: does רבי אליעזר really hold that a breach alone turns a private courtyard into a full רשות הרבים?
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: And according to רבי אליעזר, just because the courtyard was breached into the public domain, does it become a public domain?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins discussing the משנה. It questions how רבי אליעזר can make such a big jump, and this sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The courtyard still belongs to a private owner. It just has a gap in its wall. It sounds strange that this alone would make it fully public, so the גמרא asks what reasoning supports רבי אליעזר.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmud's discussion that follows the משנה (marked here as גְּמָ׳)
It was breached; a gap was opened in the wall

phrases.english: GEMARA:
And according to Rabbi Eliezer,
because it was breached into the public domain
does it become a public domain?!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר, מִשּׁוּם דְּנִפְרְצָה לִרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים הָוְיָא לַהּ רְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא's analysis by questioning the logic behind רבי אליעזר's ruling in the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What reasoning lets רבי אליעזר say that a privately owned courtyard becomes a רשות הרבים just because it was breached?

steps.title: Yes, this follows רבי אליעזר's own reasoning
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says yes, that really is his view, because רבי אליעזר is consistent with a view he holds elsewhere.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes. רבי אליעזר follows his own reasoning.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא confirms that רבי אליעזר really holds this. It says this fits his general approach, and the next step will show where that approach comes from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Calling a view לטעמיה means it is not a one-time idea. It comes from a broader principle the same Tanna holds in another place. The proof for that principle is coming next.

keyTerms.meaning: According to his own reasoning; consistent with his view elsewhere

phrases.english: Yes,
Rabbi Eliezer follows his own reasoning,

steps.triggerLanguage: אִין, רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר לְטַעְמֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 13 by tying רבי אליעזר's ruling to his broader view.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי אליעזר does hold this, because it fits his consistent view about public rights to space.

steps.title: A path the public chooses becomes theirs
steps.stepSummary: Proof from a ברייתא: רבי יהודה reports in the name of רבי אליעזר that when the public chooses a path for itself, the path they chose is theirs.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught in a ברייתא: רבי יהודה said in the name of רבי אליעזר: if the public chose a path for themselves, what they chose, they chose.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the source showing רבי אליעזר's general approach. Once the public uses a space, it gains public rights there, even on private land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the public can take over a path through someone's field just by choosing it, then a breached courtyard that the public can walk into can also become public space. This is how רבי אליעזר can call the breached courtyard a full רשות הרבים.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was taught (introduces a ברייתא)

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא, רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר:
phrases.english: As it was taught: Rabbi Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Eliezer:
if the public chose a path for themselves,
what they chose, they chose (it is theirs).

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא, רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source for the 'לטעמיה' claim in Step 14.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי אליעזר holds that public use can create public rights over private space.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא in which רבי יהודה quotes רבי אליעזר: a path the public chose for itself belongs to the public.
steps.whyThisMatters: This ברייתא is the foundation for רבי אליעזר's ruling in the משנה. The next step will test whether it really says what we need.

steps.title: רב limits the ברייתא to a lost path
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the proof. רב גידל quotes רב as saying the ברייתא applies only when the public had lost an existing path in that field.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so?! But didn't רב גידל say in the name of רב: this applies only when they had lost a path in that field.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof from Step 15. It shows that the ברייתא may be much narrower than it first seemed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רב, the public cannot just take a path through private land. They only get to choose a new route when there already was a public path in that field and its exact location was forgotten. If so, the ברייתא does not show a general rule that public use creates public rights, so it may not support רבי אליעזר's view about the breached courtyard.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that so?! (an expression of surprise that opens a challenge)
But didn't he say...? (introduces a contradicting statement)
That it was lost to them

phrases.english: Is that so?!
But didn't Rav Giddel say that Rav said:
and this applies only when a path had been lost to them
in that field.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִינִי? וְהָאָמַר רַב גִּידֵּל אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the proof of Step 15 by narrowing what the ברייתא actually means.
steps.kashyaTarget: The use of the ברייתא of 'רבים שבררו דרך' as a source for רבי אליעזר's ruling about the breached courtyard.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב limits the ברייתא to a case where an older public path existed and was lost. So the ברייתא does not prove that the public can create new public rights over private space, which is what the breached courtyard case needs.
steps.confusionAlert: רב is not arguing with רבי אליעזר's ruling about the courtyard. He is only explaining the ברייתא more narrowly, and that weakens the proof from it.

steps.title: Can the משנה also be a lost-path case? רבי חנינא says no
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests our משנה might also be about a lost public path. It then challenges this with רבי חנינא, who says the dispute covers the courtyard all the way up to the place of the wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say: here too, in our משנה, the case is where the public lost a path in that courtyard. But didn't רבי חנינא say: the dispute extends up to the place of the partition?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a possible way to explain the משנה: maybe it is also a lost-path case. It immediately pushes back using a statement of רבי חנינא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the משנה were only about a lost path, רבי אליעזר would call only that strip public domain. But רבי חנינא says the argument covers the courtyard 'עַד' (up to) the wall's location. That means the whole courtyard, not just a strip, so the lost-path reading seems not to fit.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you will say (the גמרא raises a possible answer)
The public lost track of a path they once had
Up to the place of the partition, covering the whole area until the wall line

phrases.english: And if you say: here too (in our Mishnah)
the case is where the public lost a path
in that courtyard,
but didn't Rabbi Ḥanina say:
phrases.notes: Introduces the challenge

phrases.english: the dispute extends up to the place of the partition.
phrases.notes: Implies the whole courtyard is under dispute

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא: הָכָא נָמֵי כְּגוֹן שֶׁאָבְדָה לָהֶן דֶּרֶךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies רב's lost-path limit from Step 16 to our משנה, then challenges that application.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that our משנה is a lost-path case
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי חנינא's word 'עד' shows the dispute covers the entire courtyard, not just a lost strip.

steps.title: Re-reading רבי חנינא: the dispute is only on the wall's spot
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes one word in רבי חנינא's statement, from עַד ('up to') to עַל ('on'). Now the dispute covers only the spot where the wall stood.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say instead: the dispute is about the place of the partition itself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by reading רבי חנינא's statement differently. With the new reading, the lost-path explanation of the משנה works again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With 'עַל', רבי חנינא is saying the dispute is only about the strip where the wall used to stand. That is exactly where a lost public path could have run. So רבי אליעזר does not make the whole courtyard public, only that strip.

keyTerms.meaning: On the place of the partition, meaning only that spot

steps.confusionAlert: Only one small word changes: עַד ('up to') becomes עַל ('on'). That single word shrinks the dispute from the whole courtyard down to just the strip where the wall was.

phrases.english: Say instead: the dispute is about the place of the partition itself.
phrases.notes: עַל replaces עַד

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵימָא: עַל מְקוֹם מְחִיצָה מַחֲלוֹקֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from רבי חנינא.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי חנינא meant the whole courtyard is under dispute.
steps.terutzMaskana: The dispute is only about the strip where the wall stood, so the lost-path reading of the משנה holds.

steps.title: Second explanation: the edges of a public domain
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא offers another explanation. רבי אליעזר holds that the edges of a public domain count as public domain, and the רבנן hold they do not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or if you prefer, say: they disagree about the edges of a public domain. רבי אליעזר holds that the edges of a public domain are like a public domain. The רבנן hold that the edges of a public domain are not like a public domain.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a whole new reason for רבי אליעזר's view that does not need any lost path. The wall's old spot sits at the edge of the street, and the question is whether street edges count as the street.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this approach, everyone may know exactly where the wall stood. The disagreement is a general rule about edges of public space. רבי אליעזר treats the breach area as part of the street, and the רבנן do not.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say (introduces an alternative answer)
The sides or edges of a public domain

steps.whyThisMatters: צִידֵּי רְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים is a well-known topic in הלכות שבת. This step ties our משנה to that broader question.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
they disagree about the sides of a public domain,
for Rabbi Eliezer holds:

phrases.aramaic: צִידֵּי רְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים — כִּרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים דָּמוּ,
phrases.english: the sides of a public domain are like a public domain,
and the Rabbis hold:

phrases.aramaic: צִידֵּי רְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים — לָאו כִּרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים דָּמוּ.
phrases.english: the sides of a public domain are not like a public domain.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא, בְּצִידֵּי רְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים קָמִיפַּלְגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second, independent answer to the question of Step 13.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי אליעזר's view must depend on a lost public path.
steps.terutzMaskana: It can instead rest on his view that the edges of a public domain are public domain.

steps.title: Why not state the dispute about edges in general?
steps.stepSummary: If the argument is really about street edges, the גמרא asks why the משנה did not present it as a general case about edges.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then let them disagree about the edges of a public domain in general!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the second explanation by asking about how the משנה chose its case. It is setting up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the real topic is street edges, a plain street-edge case would have been the natural example. Choosing a breached courtyard seems like an indirect way to teach the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Then let them disagree (about a different case)
In general, in an ordinary case

phrases.english: Then let them disagree about the sides of a public domain in general?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלִיפְלוֹג בְּצִידֵּי רְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים בְּעָלְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the second explanation from Step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's choice of a breached-courtyard case
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the dispute is about edges in general, a general edge case would be the obvious example.

steps.title: The breached courtyard shows the dispute applies even without stakes
steps.stepSummary: Had the dispute been stated about edges in general, we might think the רבנן disagree only where stakes block the edges. The breached-courtyard case teaches that they disagree even with no stakes.
steps.simpleTranslation: If they had disagreed about the edges of a public domain in general, we would have said: when do the רבנן disagree with רבי אליעזר? Only where there are stakes. But where there are no stakes, say they agree with him. So the משנה teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the משנה chose the breached-courtyard case. That case teaches something a general edge case would not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Along ordinary street edges there are often stakes by the houses (חיפופי) that keep people from walking there. That would explain why the רבנן say edges are not public. A breached courtyard has no stakes at all. The רבנן still say it is not public domain, which shows their view holds in every case.

keyTerms.meaning: Stakes placed along the sides of houses that block foot traffic
These words apply (only in a certain case)
It teaches us (something we would not have known)

steps.whatToRemember: There are two explanations of רבי אליעזר. (1) The משנה is a lost-path case, limited to the spot where the wall stood (reading 'עַל'). (2) He holds that the edges of a public domain count as public domain. The breached-courtyard case shows the רבנן disagree even where there are no stakes.

phrases.aramaic: אִי אִיפְּלִיגוּ בְּצִידֵּי רְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים בְּעָלְמָא,
phrases.english: If they had disagreed about the sides of a public domain in general,
we would have said:

phrases.aramaic: כִּי פְּלִיגִי רַבָּנַן עֲלֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר —
phrases.english: when do the Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Eliezer?
only where there are stakes,
phrases.notes: Stakes make the edges unusable for walking

phrases.english: but where there are no stakes,
say they agree with him;
so it teaches us (that they disagree even then).

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי אִיפְּלִיגוּ בְּצִידֵּי רְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים בְּעָלְמָא, הֲוָה אָמְרִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: shows what the chosen case uniquely teaches
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The רבנן disagree only where stakes block the edges.
steps.terutzMaskana: The רבנן disagree even with no stakes, as in a breached courtyard.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר's own words say 'from inside'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the edges explanation. רבי אליעזר said 'מתוכה', which sounds like the whole courtyard, not just the edge.
steps.simpleTranslation: But he said 'from inside it'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the explanation from step 19. If רבי אליעזר is only talking about the edge of the street, why does he use the word 'מתוכה', from inside the courtyard?
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to step 19, רבי אליעזר treats only the strip next to the street (the edge) as רשות הרבים. But the word 'מתוכה' sounds like carrying from anywhere inside the courtyard. That would mean he treats the whole courtyard as רשות הרבים, which does not match the edges explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: But look! (opens a challenge from the text)

phrases.english: But he says 'from inside it'!
phrases.notes: 'He' is רבי אליעזר, who rules that one who carries from inside the courtyard into a private domain is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא ״מִתּוֹכָהּ״ קָאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the edges explanation (steps 19–21) from the wording of רבי אליעזר's ruling in the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רבי אליעזר only treats the edges of the public domain as public domain
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'מתוכה' implies the entire inside of the courtyard, not just the edge strip, so the edges reading does not fit his words.

steps.title: He borrowed the רבנן's wording
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר used 'מתוכה' only because the רבנן used that word. It does not tell us he means the whole courtyard.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since the רבנן said 'from inside it', he also said 'from inside it'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. רבי אליעזר just used the same word the רבנן used, so we cannot learn anything from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'מתוכה' really belongs to the רבנן's statement. רבי אליעזר's ruling is phrased with matching wording, but he really means only the edge strip. So the edges explanation still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: since / because of (the other side's wording)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not take this to mean רבי אליעזר agrees with the רבנן. Only the wording is shared. His ruling about the edge is still the opposite of theirs.

phrases.english: Since the Rabbis said 'from inside it',
he also said 'from inside it'.
phrases.notes: It is a borrowed word. It does not mean the whole courtyard for רבי אליעזר.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַיְּידֵי דַּאֲמוּר רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording challenge of step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Stylistic explanation: the wording copies the other opinion's language
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'מתוכה' shows רבי אליעזר means the whole courtyard
steps.terutzMaskana: The word was borrowed from the רבנן. רבי אליעזר means only the edge.

steps.title: The רבנן's answer seems to miss his point
steps.stepSummary: If רבי אליעזר spoke about the edges of the street, why do the רבנן answer him by talking about the inside of the courtyard?
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן: רבי אליעזר spoke about the edges of the public domain, and they reply to him with 'from inside it'!
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא raises a problem from the other side. If רבי אליעזר was talking about the edges, the רבנן's reply about 'מתוכה' seems to be about a different case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 23 said רבי אליעזר only meant the edge strip. But then the רבנן, who say 'from inside it ... exempt', seem to be talking about the inner courtyard. They never directly answer his claim about the edges. A reply should address the same case, so this looks like a mismatch.

keyTerms.meaning: the sides/edges of the public domain

phrases.english: And the Rabbis — Rabbi Eliezer said
phrases.notes: 'And the רבנן' means: now there is a difficulty with the רבנן's statement.

phrases.english: 'the sides of the public domain' (are public domain),
and they answer him back with 'from inside it'!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבָּנַן, אָמַר רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר צִידֵּי רְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 23 settled רבי אליעזר's wording, this step challenges the wording of the רבנן's reply.
steps.kashyaTarget: The edges explanation, as it applies to the רבנן's response in the משנה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A reply should address the same case. רבי אליעזר spoke of edges, but the רבנן answer about the inside of the courtyard, which seems irrelevant.

steps.title: The רבנן argue by comparison: edges are like the courtyard
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן are making a comparison. רבי אליעזר agrees that the inside of the courtyard is a כרמלית, so the edges of the street should be the same.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what the רבנן are saying to רבי אליעזר: Don't you agree with us that where one carried from inside it to the public domain, or from the public domain into it, he is exempt, because it is a כרמלית? The edges are also no different.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that the רבנן's reply is on topic after all. They point to a case רבי אליעזר already agrees with and say the edges are just like it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides agree that carrying between the breached courtyard and the street is exempt, because the courtyard is a כרמלית, not a true public domain. The רבנן use this shared point against רבי אליעזר. The edges of the street are like that courtyard, so they should also be a כרמלית. This makes the 'מתוכה' reply a real argument about the edges, so the edges explanation from step 19 holds up.

keyTerms.meaning: this is what they are saying to him
an in-between area, neither fully public nor fully private. Carrying there is forbidden only by the רבנן, not by Torah law.

steps.whatToRemember: The edges explanation survives both wording challenges. רבי אליעזר's 'מתוכה' is borrowed language. The רבנן's 'מתוכה' is a comparison: just as the courtyard is a כרמלית (which רבי אליעזר agrees to), so are the edges of the street.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a common pattern in גמרא arguments. One side uses a point the other side already agrees with to argue about the case in dispute.

phrases.aramaic: הָכִי קָאָמְרִי לֵיהּ רַבָּנַן לְרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר:
phrases.english: This is what the Rabbis are saying to Rabbi Eliezer:
Don't you agree with us
where he carried from inside it (the courtyard) to the public domain,
or from the public domain into it —
that he is exempt, because it is a כרמלית?
phrases.notes: This is the point רבי אליעזר already agrees with.

phrases.english: The edges are also no different.
phrases.notes: The comparison: the edges should also be a כרמלית.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי קָאָמְרִי לֵיהּ רַבָּנַן לְרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 24 by reading the רבנן's statement as a comparison that addresses the edges directly.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of the reply as an argument from an agreed-upon case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The רבנן's 'מתוכה' is about a different case and does not answer רבי אליעזר
steps.terutzMaskana: The רבנן cite the agreed case (the courtyard is a כרמלית) to show that the edges should be a כרמלית too

steps.title: רבי אליעזר rejects the comparison: the public walks on the street edges
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר answers the רבנן. Their comparison fails because nobody from the public walks inside a courtyard, but the public does walk on the edges of the street.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי אליעזר? There (inside the courtyard), the public does not walk on it. Here (the edges of the street), the public does walk on it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how רבי אליעזר answers the comparison the רבנן made in the last step. He points to one real difference between the two places.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן said that if the inside of a breached courtyard is a כרמלית, then the edges of the street should be one too. רבי אליעזר says the cases are not alike. Crowds really walk on the street edges, so those edges act like full רשות הרבים. Nobody walks through the inside of the courtyard.

keyTerms.meaning: They tread on it; they walk over it
There / here. Used to contrast two cases

steps.whatToRemember: For רבי אליעזר, what makes a place רשות הרבים is real foot traffic from the public. The edges of a street have that traffic. The inside of a courtyard does not.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Eliezer (how does he answer?)
phrases.notes: The question is implied: how does he answer the רבנן's comparison?

phrases.aramaic: הָתָם לָא קָא דָרְסִי לַהּ רַבִּים,
phrases.english: there, the public does not walk on it
phrases.notes: There = the inside of the breached courtyard

phrases.english: here, the public does walk on it.
phrases.notes: Here = the edges of the public street

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר, הָתָם לָא קָא דָרְסִי לַהּ רַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the comparison the רבנן made in step 25
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the comparison between the inside of the courtyard and the edges of the street
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The comparison ignores real public foot traffic. The street edges have it and the courtyard does not.

steps.title: New משנה: places that lost their walls on שבת, רבי יהודה's view
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה starts. רבי יהודה rules on three cases: a courtyard breached on two sides, a house breached on two sides, and an alleyway whose קורה or לחי was removed. Carrying is permitted for that שבת but forbidden in the future.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: A courtyard that was broken open to the public domain on two of its sides. Likewise a house broken open on two sides. Likewise an alleyway whose crossbeams or side posts were taken away. They are permitted for that שבת and forbidden for the future. These are the words of רבי יהודה.
steps.whatsHappening: A brand-new משנה begins with a new topic. רבי יהודה rules about places whose walls or markers were removed on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, carrying in a courtyard or an alleyway needs proper walls or markers, such as a קורה or a לחי. רבי יהודה says that if these are lost during שבת, you may still carry for the rest of that שבת. Starting from the next שבת, it is forbidden until they are fixed.

keyTerms.meaning: An alleyway shared by several courtyards
A crossbeam / a side post. These markers allow carrying in an alleyway
In the future, meaning on later שבתות

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'לעתיד לבא' just means future שבתות. It has nothing to do with the messianic era.

phrases.english: MISHNA: A courtyard that was breached into the public domain
on two of its sides,
and likewise a house that was breached on two of its sides,

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵן מָבוֹי שֶׁנִּטְּלוּ קוֹרוֹתָיו אוֹ לְחָיָיו —
phrases.english: and likewise an alleyway whose crossbeams or side posts were removed —
they are permitted on that Shabbat,
and forbidden in the future,
these are the words of Rabbi Yehuda.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ חָצֵר שֶׁנִּפְרְצָה לִרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים מִשְׁתֵּי רוּחוֹתֶיהָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה and a new topic
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Places that lost their walls or alleyway markers on שבת stay permitted for that שבת but are forbidden afterward

steps.title: רבי יוסי: this שבת and future שבתות must have the same rule
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי disagrees with רבי יהודה. If carrying is permitted on that שבת, it is permitted in the future too. If it is forbidden in the future, it is forbidden on that שבת too.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי says: If they are permitted for that שבת, they are permitted for the future. And if they are forbidden for the future, they are forbidden for that שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה brings רבי יוסי's opposing view. He refuses to split the rule between this שבת and future ones.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה holds that what was permitted when שבת began stays permitted all that שבת. רבי יוסי says the place's status depends only on how it looks now. So the rule cannot be different for this שבת and the next one.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא who disagrees with רבי יהודה here

steps.whatToRemember: The argument is whether a place that was permitted when שבת began can stay permitted after its walls are lost. רבי יהודה says yes, for that שבת only. רבי יוסי says no: the rule must be the same for now and later.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says:
if they are permitted for that Shabbat —
they are permitted for the future,
and if they are forbidden for the future —
they are forbidden for that Shabbat.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר: אִם מוּתָּרִין לְאוֹתוֹ שַׁבָּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing opinion to רבי יהודה in the same משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The rule for that שבת and for future שבתות must match

steps.title: What case is the משנה talking about?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens by asking what kind of breach the משנה means.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: What case are we dealing with?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts its discussion by asking exactly what case the משנה describes. This sets up the next two steps, which test two possible breach sizes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says 'breached on two sides' but never says how wide the breach is. Width matters a lot, so the גמרא needs to pin down the case before it can make sense of the ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with?

phrases.english: GEMARA: With what case are we dealing?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא's analysis of the משנה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How wide is the breach the משנה is describing?

steps.title: A breach of up to ten is just a doorway, even on two sides
steps.stepSummary: Suppose the breach is up to ten אמות wide. On one side we call that a doorway, so on two sides it should simply be two doorways. Then why would two sides make a difference?
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say it is a breach of ten: how is it different from one side, where we say 'it is a doorway'? On two sides, too, it is a doorway!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the first option: a breach of up to ten אמות. It shows that this option does not fit the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A gap of up to ten אמות in a wall counts as a פתח (doorway), which does not ruin the walls. Two such gaps would just be two doorways. So under this option, the משנה would have no reason to say that a breach on two sides causes a problem.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (introduces a possible explanation that will be tested)
A doorway, which does not ruin the walls

phrases.english: If you say it is with a breach of ten,
how is it different from a breach on one side,
where we say: it is a doorway?
On two sides as well, it is a doorway!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִילֵימָא בְּעֶשֶׂר, מַאי שְׁנָא מֵרוּחַ אַחַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the first possible answer to the question in step 29
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that the משנה is talking about a breach of up to ten אמות
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A gap of up to ten is a doorway. Two doorways are no worse than one, so two sides should not matter.

steps.title: A breach of more than ten should be a problem even on one side
steps.stepSummary: So the breach must be more than ten אמות. But a gap that big ruins the walls even on one side, so why does the משנה say 'two sides'?
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is a breach of more than ten. If so, even on one side it should be forbidden too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the second option: a breach of more than ten אמות. This option also clashes with the משנה, which leaves the גמרא stuck and needing a new answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A gap wider than ten אמות is a real breach, not a doorway, and it cancels the walls. If so, even one breach like that should be enough to cause the problem. The משנה's detail of 'two sides' would then be unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: More than ten (אמות). A real breach, not a doorway

steps.confusionAlert: Both options have now failed. This is not the conclusion. The גמרא is about to suggest a different way to read the משנה.

phrases.english: Rather, it is with a breach of more than ten,

phrases.aramaic: אִי הָכִי — אֲפִילּוּ מֵרוּחַ אַחַת נָמֵי!
phrases.english: if so — even on one side as well (it should be forbidden)!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא בְּיָתֵר מֵעֶשֶׂר, אִי הָכִי אֲפִילּוּ מֵרוּחַ אַחַת נָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After rejecting the first option, tests the second option and attacks it too
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that the משנה is talking about a breach of more than ten אמות
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A breach of more than ten ruins the walls even on one side. So the משנה's 'two sides' would add nothing.

steps.title: רב says the breach is really up to ten אמות
steps.stepSummary: רב answers the difficulty by saying the משנה is talking about a breach of up to ten אמות. He still has to explain why two sides make a difference.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: Really, the משנה is talking about a breach of up to ten אמות.
steps.whatsHappening: רב begins his answer by picking the first option: the breach is up to ten אמות wide. This line sets up the answer, and the next words will explain why breaches on two sides still cause a problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word לעולם means "really" or "actually." It tells us רב is going back to an option the גמרא already pushed away, the breach of up to ten אמות. That option was rejected in Step 30 because a gap that size usually counts as a doorway. So רב must add a detail that shows why this breach does not count as a doorway when it is on two sides.

keyTerms.meaning: רב said. רב is an early אמורא, and his statement brings the answer here.
Really, actually. Used when the גמרא goes back to an option it seemed to have rejected.
With ten, meaning a breach of up to ten אמות wide.
A breach, a gap in a wall. This is the subject of the whole question.

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רב is saying the earlier question was wrong. He agrees that a breach of up to ten אמות on one side is fine. He is about to add a detail about where the breach is that changes the result when it is on two sides.

phrases.english: Rav said:
phrases.notes: The attribution leads straight into רב's answer.

phrases.english: Actually, it is talking about a breach of up to ten cubits,
phrases.notes: לעולם tells us he is going back to the first option from Step 30. The comma shows that his explanation continues in the next part.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב: לְעוֹלָם בְּעֶשֶׂר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Steps 30-31 seemed to close off both possible sizes of breach. רב answers by going back to the first option, a breach of up to ten אמות.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defines the case. רב picks the up-to-ten size and will add a detail about where the breach is.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A breach of up to ten אמות always counts as a doorway, so two sides could never matter.
steps.terutzMaskana: The breach is up to ten אמות. The way it is placed, explained next, explains why two sides matter.
